nameStory: The name 'selfheal' comes from this plant's legendary ability to heal wounds and ailments all by itself - no doctor needed! Folk herbalists believed it could cure just about anything, earning it the nickname 'heal-all.' The scientific name Prunella comes from a German word for a throat disease this plant was thought to cure.
description: Common selfheal is a low-growing perennial herb that spreads along the ground, rarely reaching more than a foot tall. It's a member of the mint family with the characteristic square stems and opposite leaves. The most distinctive feature is its dense, purple flower spike that looks like a small pinecone sitting atop the stem. You'll often find it forming patches in lawns, fields, and disturbed areas throughout New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, cylindrical purple flower spikes about 1-2 inches long that look like small pinecones. Individual flowers are small, tubular, and violet-purple, emerging from between papery brown bracts that feel dry and rustly to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along square stems. Leaves feel slightly fuzzy and have a mild minty smell when crushed, with smooth or slightly toothed edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low mats by spreading along the ground with creeping stems that root at the joints. Flower stalks rise 4-12 inches above the spreading leafy base.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctly four-sided (square) stems that are characteristic of the mint family. Run your fingers along them to feel the sharp edges at each corner.

habitat: Common selfheal thrives in disturbed soils, lawns, roadsides, fields, and woodland edges throughout New England. It prefers moist, fertile soil but tolerates poor conditions and partial shade. You'll often find it mixed with grasses and other weedy plants in areas with regular foot traffic or mowing.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge early, forming low green mats. Young square stems begin growing upward as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with distinctive purple flower spikes appearing from June through August. This is when the plant is most easily identified.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and leaves may turn reddish. Seeds mature and disperse, while the plant continues spreading via creeping stems.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level in most areas, but may persist as small evergreen rosettes in protected spots or milder locations.

funFact: This humble little plant has been used medicinally for over 2,000 years and was so valued that it was one of the first plants European colonists intentionally brought to North America - it literally traveled across the ocean in their medicine chests!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with other small purple-flowered lawn weeds like ground ivy or wild mint. The key difference is selfheal's distinctive cone-like flower spike - other mints have flowers in loose clusters or whorls around the stem, not packed into a dense cylindrical head.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its many folk medicine uses, selfheal is considered safe and is still used in some herbal preparations today. The plant is also known by many colorful common names including 'carpenter's herb' (supposedly because carpenters used it to treat cuts) and 'heart-of-the-earth.'
compareHints: Common selfheal is the only member of the Prunella genus found in New England. Compared to other mints in the family, it's unique for its dense, cone-like flower clusters - most other mints have their flowers arranged in whorls around the stem or in loose spikes. The combination of creeping growth habit and distinctive flower shape makes it quite different from typical upright mints like spearmint or peppermint.
